summary: Describes a SOCKS-based gateway mechanism that lets IPv6-only and IPv4-only hosts communicate. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: One person speaks English and another speaks French. This is an interpreter in the middle so the old and new Internet addresses can chat.

questions: how to connect ipv6 and ipv4 hosts
subtitle: How to let IPv4-only and IPv6-only hosts talk to each other across the address gap

tldr.problem: As the internet transitions from IPv4 to IPv6, some hosts are IPv4-only and others are IPv6-only. An IPv4 application cannot understand a 128-bit IPv6 address (it only has a 4-byte space), making direct communication impossible.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC describes a SOCKS-based gateway that relays two 'terminated' IPv4 and IPv6 connections at the application layer. The gateway runs on a dual-stack node (supporting both IPv4 and IPv6), and 'socksified' client applications intercept their socket calls to route through the gateway.
tldr.outcome: Applications can communicate across the IPv4/IPv6 boundary without modification, by linking a SOCKS library that redirects socket and DNS calls to the gateway, which handles the address translation transparently.

today: RFC 3089 is an Informational RFC and remains the specification for the SOCKS-based IPv6/IPv4 gateway mechanism. It describes implementations available from NEC and Fujitsu Lab (SOCKS64), and provides a transition path for applications in the IPv4-to-IPv6 migration period.

sections.title: The Gateway Architecture
sections.content:
The SOCKS-based IPv6/IPv4 gateway mechanism enables heterogeneous communications between IPv6 nodes and IPv4 nodes without introducing new protocols. It builds on SOCKS version 5 (RFC 1928), which was originally designed for firewall traversal. The mechanism works by relaying two 'terminated' connections at the application layer, maintaining separate IPv4 and IPv6 connections on each side of the gateway.

The architecture introduces two functional blocks: a SOCKS Lib installed on client systems that intercepts socket and DNS calls, and a Gateway running on a dual-stack node (supporting both IPv4 and IPv6). The client makes a 'socksified' connection (control and data) to the gateway, and the gateway makes a normal connection to the destination. The gateway does not introduce new protocols; it applies the native SOCKS mechanism to heterogeneous communications, providing the same appearance and functionality.
sections.plainLanguage: A client library on each computer pretends to be the normal connection system, but secretly sends messages through an interpreter (the gateway) that knows both IPv4 and IPv6 languages.

sections.title: Connection Types and Packet Handling
sections.content:
The mechanism supports four combinations of IPv4 and IPv6: IPv4 to IPv4 (handled by normal SOCKS), IPv4 to IPv6 (heterogeneous), IPv6 to IPv4 (heterogeneous), and IPv6 to IPv6 (handled by SOCKS extension). Since the IPv6 header is 40 bytes and the IPv4 header is 20 bytes, packet size differences must be managed. The application-layer relay naturally handles this: the relayed data is a simple stream at the application layer, and each relayed connection side adjusts packet size independently, never exceeding MTU.

The SOCKS-based approach provides authenticated relay through native SOCKS authentication methods (no new auth protocols needed), and maintains the same application API to the client, requiring only 'socksification' (relinking with the SOCKS library) rather than modifying application source code.
sections.plainLanguage: When IPv4 and IPv6 packets pass through the interpreter, their sizes adjust automatically because they're being translated at the message level, not just wrapped at the network level.

sections.title: DNS Name Resolving Delegation
sections.content:
The critical problem with heterogeneous communications is that an IPv4 application cannot store an IPv6 address (it only has 4 bytes of address space). The RFC solves this through 'DNS name resolving delegation': the client's DNS lookups are delegated to the dual-stack gateway, which can resolve both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. The gateway uses 'fake IP' addresses (from a reserved space like 0.0.0.x) as temporary placeholders. The SOCKS Lib maintains a mapping table linking each fake IP to the actual fully-qualified domain name (FQDN).

When an application calls DNS functions (like gethostbyname()), the SOCKS Lib intercepts it and returns a fake IP from the reserved space instead of calling the real DNS. When the application later uses that fake IP in a socket call, the SOCKS Lib looks up the real FQDN from the mapping table and sends it to the gateway via the SOCKS protocol. The gateway then performs the actual DNS lookup and creates the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of trying to give the application an IPv6 number (which it cannot store), the client library gives it a fake number, remembers what the real name was, and tells the gateway the real name when connecting.

sections.title: Multiple Relay Chains and Applicability
sections.content:
The mechanism supports multiple chained relay topologies, allowing more complex IPv4/IPv6 mixed network topologies. Multiple gateways can be chained: a client can socks-ify its gateway, allowing the gateway itself to relay through another gateway. While this adds complexity, it enables scenarios where only specific protocols or topologies are available.

The mechanism requires only 'socksification' of applications, not modification of their source code—typically done by relinking dynamic libraries. It does not require modifying the DNS system or network infrastructure. However, there are three types of constraints: (1) essential constraints from address length differences (functions returning IP addresses like getpeername() cannot provide correct IPv6 addresses), (2) SOCKS mechanism limitations with tricky applications using extraordinary connection methods, and (3) constraints that fake addresses must be treated as temporary values, though storing them permanently causes only harmless failures since they are from reserved space.
sections.plainLanguage: Multiple interpreters can be chained if needed for complex network setups. Applications don't need source code changes, just relinking libraries. The main limitation is that programs cannot store or save IPv6 addresses.

sections.title: Security and Protocol Considerations
sections.content:
The SOCKS-based IPv6/IPv4 gateway mechanism inherits the security features of SOCKSv5 protocol. Since the mechanism relays two terminated connections at the application layer, end-to-end security is maintained at each relayed connection (client to gateway, and gateway to destination), but not as a single end-to-end path from the original source to final destination.

The SOCKSv5 protocol defines three commands: CONNECT (the main command for TCP connections, with no weak points), BIND (designed for FTP reverse-channel rendezvous, not suitable for general use), and UDP ASSOCIATE (designed for simple UDP applications like archie, not general enough for mixed TCP/UDP applications). When using BIND or UDP ASSOCIATE in the gateway mechanism, these limitations must be considered.
sections.plainLanguage: Security works the same as regular SOCKS: the connection to the interpreter is locked, and the interpreter-to-destination connection is locked. But these are two separate locks, not one continuous lock from start to end.
